Christopher Wren. The English polymath—mathematician, astronomer, and architect—whose work defined English Baroque architecture and reshaped London after its greatest catastrophe.

Sir Christopher Wren lived from 1632 to 1723. His most famous work is St. Paul's Cathedral, which he designed and oversaw construction of between 1668 and 1710. It's a Baroque masterpiece featuring a soaring dome and classical portico that became London's most iconic building. Following the Great Fire of London in 1666, Wren rebuilt over fifty churches in the city. Each one is a small jewel of Baroque design, and together they established a coherent architectural style for post-fire London.

Beyond these religious commissions, Wren designed the Royal Observatory in Greenwich in 1675, combining scientific function with architectural elegance and establishing a new typology for scientific buildings. He designed secular buildings too, including additions to Kensington Palace and the Royal Naval College at Greenwich, expanding his range beyond religious architecture.

Wren studied mathematics and astronomy, bringing scientific rigor and geometric proportion to his designs. His City churches, small urban parish churches built with economy and elegance, became models for sacred architecture. Many of them still stand and are in use today. Wren pioneered the use of classical orders and Baroque ornament in English architecture, adapting continental European style to English tradition. His work connects directly to earlier dome design—Filippo Brunelleschi's Florence dome influenced Wren's St. Paul's. He was the defining figure of English Baroque, adapting continental style to the English context.
